stem: A 68-year-old man with hypertension and obesity presents to the emergency department with palpitations and mild dyspnea on exertion that began 4 hours ago. He is alert and conversational. Vital signs: BP 138/82 mmHg, HR 138 bpm and irregularly irregular, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air. Cardiac auscultation reveals an irregularly irregular rhythm without a murmur. Lung exam is clear. He has no history of heart failure, no preserved- or reduced-EF cardiomyopathy on prior echocardiogram (LVEF 60% one year ago), and no Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome on baseline ECG. ECG today confirms atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response (rate 138 bpm) and no pre-excitation.
question: Which is the most appropriate first-line intravenous agent for acute rate control in this patient?

options.C: IV adenosine 6 mg, escalating to 12 mg if needed

rationale: For acute rate control in stable atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response in a patient WITHOUT heart failure, pre-excitation, or hypotension, both intravenous beta-blockers (e.g., metoprolol) and non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil) are Class I recommendations per the 2023 ACC/AHA AFib Guideline. Diltiazem provides rapid onset and predictable rate reduction. Digoxin (option B) has slow onset (hours) and is reserved for second-line use or for patients with concomitant HF when beta-blockers and CCBs are insufficient or not tolerated. Adenosine (option C) is used for terminating supraventricular tachycardias dependent on AV-node conduction (e.g., AVNRT) — it does NOT control rate in AFib because the multiple atrial wavefronts continue. Amiodarone (option D) is a rhythm-control agent and is generally not first-line for rate control in stable AFib without underlying HF.

variants.stem_override: A 68-year-old man with non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (LVEF 28% on echocardiogram one month ago) on chronic guideline-directed medical therapy (sacubitril/valsartan, carvedilol 12.5 mg BID, spironolactone, dapagliflozin) presents to the emergency department with palpitations and mild dyspnea that began 4 hours ago. He is alert and conversational. Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 138 bpm and irregularly irregular, RR 20, SpO2 96% on room air. Lung exam shows mild bibasilar crackles. ECG confirms atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response (rate 138 bpm) and no pre-excitation.
variants.rationale_for_variant: Mixed perturbation — adds HFrEF (LVEF 28%) on chronic GDMT. Non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil) are CONTRAINDICATED in HFrEF because of negative inotropy that can precipitate decompensation; this is a Class III recommendation in the 2023 ACC/AHA AFib Guideline. The appropriate first-line acute rate-control agent in HFrEF is an intravenous beta-blocker (e.g., metoprolol or esmolol, used cautiously). The correct answer therefore shifts away from diltiazem; in this option set, IV digoxin (option B) is the most appropriate of the listed choices because it preserves negative inotropy avoidance — a guideline-supported alternative in HFrEF when an oral beta-blocker is being titrated. Tests whether the model recognizes the diltiazem/verapamil contraindication in HFrEF.
